Exact Binomial Test, Computed as SAS Proc Freq Does

Source: R/exact_binom_test_sas.R
exact_binom_test_sas.Rd

exact_binom_test_sas() takes similar arguments as stats::binom.test() but returns the p-values that SAS Proc Freq reports for

proc freq;
  tables resp / binomial(p = <p> level = "<event>");
  exact binomial;
run;

stats::binom.test() and Proc Freq differ in how the two-sided p-value is defined in terms of:

  • how one-sided p-values are reported, and

  • how the correct tail is computed.

Each difference is described below. Only the hypothesis test is computed by this function (i.e., not automatic production of confidence intervals).

exact_binom_test_sas(
  x,
  n,
  p = 0.5,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater")
)

Arguments

x

A single whole number for the number of successes, or a vector of two whole numbers for the numbers of successes and failures, as in stats::binom.test().

n

A single whole number for the number of trials. Ignored when x has two values.

p

A single number in [0, 1] for the probability of success under the null hypothesis.

alternative

A single string for the alternative hypothesis: "two.sided" (the default), "less", or "greater".

Value

An object of class htest with the same elements as the result of stats::binom.test(), except conf.int:

  • statistic: the number of successes.

  • parameter: the number of trials.

  • p.value: the p-value, as Proc Freq reports it. It is NA for a one-sided alternative when the requested tail is not the smaller one.

  • estimate: the sample proportion, x / n.

  • null.value: p.

  • alternative, method, and data.name: strings that describe the test.

Details

Notation

Let \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p_0)\), where \(p_0\) is p, and let \(x\) be the observed number of successes. The two one-sided p-values are the tails

$$ p_L = \Pr(X \le x) = \sum_{k=0}^{x} \binom{n}{k} p_0^k (1 - p_0)^{n - k} $$

$$ p_R = \Pr(X \ge x) = \sum_{k=x}^{n} \binom{n}{k} p_0^k (1 - p_0)^{n - k} $$

One-sided p-values

Proc Freq computes both tails but reports only the smaller one:

  • When \(p_L \le p_R\), the left tail is reported (XPL_BIN) and the right tail (XPR_BIN) is missing.

  • Otherwise, the right tail is reported and the left tail is missing.

exact_binom_test_sas() does the same. With alternative = "less", p.value is \(p_L\) when it is the smaller tail and NA otherwise. With alternative = "greater", p.value is \(p_R\) when it is the smaller tail and NA otherwise. Since \(p_L + p_R = 1 + \Pr(X = x) > 1\), the smaller tail is the one on the same side of \(n p_0\) as \(x\), apart from ties (see "Precision").

Two-sided p-value

The two functions define the two-sided p-value differently. In the terms of Fay (2010), SAS Proc Freq uses the "central" method: twice the smaller tail, capped at 1. This is also called "doubling" or "TST" by Hirji (2006).

For example, with \(n = 10\), \(x = 5\), and \(p_0 = 0.25\), the right tail is \(p_R = 0.0781269\) and is the smaller tail, SAS computes:

  p_2 = 2 * 0.0781269 = 0.1562538

Precision

Proc Freq computes the right tail as one minus the left tail at \(x - 1\):

$$ p_R = 1 - \Pr(X \le x - 1) $$

When \(p_R\) is small, \(\Pr(X \le x - 1)\) is close to 1 and the subtraction loses relative precision. For example, with \(n = 6\), \(x = 6\), and \(p_0 = 0.01\), \(p_R = 10^{-12}\), and SAS's value is correct to only about four significant digits instead of the usual 15 or 16. Right tails below about \(10^{-16}\) come out as exactly 0.

exact_binom_test_sas() uses the same subtraction, 1 - pbinom(x - 1, n, p), so that it returns these values too.

The results are not identical to Proc Freq's to the last bit. R's stats::pbinom() and Proc Freq use different algorithms for the binomial distribution function, and their results usually differ by a few dozen units in the last place (at most a few hundred). This is random rounding error in both, not a bias in either. Over 11,466 combinations of \(1 \le x \le n \le 50\) and \(p_0 \in \{0.01, 0.25, 0.5\}\), the p-values from exact_binom_test_sas() are within \(5.5 \times 10^{-14}\) (absolute) of Proc Freq's. Because of the cancellation, the agreement for small right tails is only absolute: a right tail that is 0 in one can be about \(10^{-16}\) in the other.

Ties

When \(p_0 = 0.5\) and \(x = n / 2\), the two tails are exactly equal, and which tail is reported depends on rounding error. Proc Freq reported the right tail for some even \(n\) and the left tail for others, and exact_binom_test_sas() can choose differently. For the 25 ties with \(n \le 50\), Proc Freq reported the right tail in 14, so the NA is on the other alternative in those cases. The reported values differ from Proc Freq's by at most \(1.2 \times 10^{-14}\), as in the cases without ties. When the computed tails are equal, the left tail is reported. The two-sided p-value is 1 either way.

References

SAS Institute Inc. "Binomial Proportion." SAS/STAT User's Guide: The FREQ Procedure.

Fay, M. P. (2010). Two-sided exact tests and matching confidence intervals for discrete data. The R Journal, 2(1), 53-58.

Hirji, K. F. (2006). Exact Analysis of Discrete Data. Chapman and Hall/CRC.

Blaker, H. (2000). Confidence curves and improved exact confidence intervals for discrete distributions. Canadian Journal of Statistics, 28(4), 783-798.

See also

stats::binom.test()

Examples

# The two-sided p-values differ by definition
exact_binom_test_sas(5, 10, p = 0.25)
#> 
#> 	Exact binomial test (SAS Proc Freq)
#> 
#> data:  5 and 10
#> number of successes = 5, number of trials = 10, p-value = 0.1563
#> alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.25
#> sample estimates:
#> probability of success 
#>                    0.5 
#> 
binom.test(5, 10, p = 0.25)$p.value
#> [1] 0.1344404

# Only the smaller tail is reported
exact_binom_test_sas(5, 10, p = 0.25, alternative = "greater")$p.value
#> [1] 0.07812691
exact_binom_test_sas(5, 10, p = 0.25, alternative = "less")$p.value
#> [1] NA

# A small right tail loses precision, as in SAS
exact_binom_test_sas(6, 6, p = 0.01, alternative = "greater")$p.value
#> [1] 9.999779e-13
binom.test(6, 6, p = 0.01, alternative = "greater")$p.value
#> [1] 1e-12
